paragraphs: Graph models can perform well on familiar data yet struggle when the data distribution changes. Causal graph learning addresses this by identifying subgraphs that support more generalizable predictions. This paper examines graph regression, where the output is a numerical value, because most existing evidence for causal graph learning comes from classification tasks.

The authors revisit how these methods handle confounders: factors whose relationships with the graph and prediction target complicate causal interpretation. Their approach explicitly considers the predictive information confounders carry in graph-level regression. This makes the treatment of confounding a central design question rather than simply transferring the procedures used for categorical predictions.

They also adapt causal intervention techniques developed for classification through a contrastive-learning perspective, which reasons about relationships between examples. Experiments on graph benchmarks involving distribution shifts support the effectiveness of the resulting proposals. The contribution is a recipe for extending causal graph learning to numerical prediction, with particular attention to how confounding and intervention should be reconsidered for that setting.
icml-2025-a-recipe-for-causal-graph-regr.tldr: The paper adapts causal graph learning to regression by reconsidering confounders and reformulating intervention techniques through contrastive learning.

paragraphs: Incomplete multi-view clustering groups samples described by several kinds of information when some views are missing. A central challenge is combining what the views share with what makes each view distinctive. BACDL is designed to capture both sources of information together, addressing methods that typically emphasize one or the other.

The algorithm first splits feature clusters and then increases their separation to make them more distinguishable. It uses distribution learning to incorporate guidance from individual views into those clusters, helping reconcile differences in feature dimensionality. This provides a way to connect heterogeneous descriptions without requiring their original feature spaces to have identical dimensions.

Its cross-view connection relies on the principle that samples belonging to a common cluster have similar marginal and conditional distributions. BACDL uses this relationship to associate feature clusters with sample clusters, then reorders and maps incomplete sample clusters into a shared clustering representation. The abstract also states that the method has linear overall overhead, making computational efficiency part of its proposed contribution.
icml-2025-bifurcate-then-alienate-incomp.tldr: BACDL combines shared and view-specific information through distribution learning to cluster incomplete multi-view data with linear overhead.

paragraphs: Designing a protein can require satisfying several requirements at once, including desired functions, sequence constraints, and structural properties. Existing protein language models described in this paper typically condition generation on a single requirement from one information type. CFP-GEN introduces a diffusion language model that combines these different constraints when generating new protein sequences.

One component adjusts the model's protein features according to combinations of functional annotations, including GO terms, IPR domains, and EC numbers. Another captures interactions at the level of individual residues, providing finer control over the generated sequence. The framework can also incorporate existing three-dimensional structure encoders to bring geometric requirements into the generation process.

The authors report high-throughput generation of novel proteins whose functionality is comparable to that of natural proteins, together with a high success rate for multifunctional designs. These findings support the approach's ability to combine functional requirements rather than handle only isolated conditions. Its main contribution is coordinating broad functional instructions, residue-level control, and structural information within one generation framework.
icml-2025-cfp-gen-combinatorial-function.tldr: CFP-GEN combines functional, sequence, and structural constraints in a diffusion language model for generating multifunctional proteins.

paragraphs: Preference training teaches a language model to favor responses people prefer, but individual tokens need not contribute equally to that preference. ConfPO targets the tokens that matter most instead of applying uniform probability adjustments throughout a response. It identifies those tokens using the confidence of the policy model currently being trained.

This selection mechanism does not require a separate credit-assignment model or an AI annotator. The method concentrates optimization on preference-critical tokens, aiming to spend its KL divergence budget more effectively. That budget describes the permitted extent of distributional change during alignment. The authors connect this more selective use of changes to improved alignment and reduced overoptimization, also called reward hacking.

Experiments across multiple language models and alignment benchmarks, including AlpacaEval 2 and Arena-Hard, show consistent improvements over uniform direct alignment algorithms. The abstract reports these gains without additional computational overhead. The practical contribution is therefore a lightweight way to make preference updates more selective using information already available from the model being optimized.
icml-2025-confpo-exploiting-policy-model.tldr: ConfPO uses the training model's confidence to target preference-critical tokens, improving reported alignment without additional computational overhead.

paragraphs: Aligning a language model with human preferences can involve expensive or unstable training. Feature-level constrained Preference Optimization, or FPO, approaches this problem through a pretrained sparse autoencoder. Such an encoder provides a feature representation in which relatively few features are active, giving the alignment procedure a sparse space in which to impose constraints.

FPO uses those active features to make preference optimization more efficient. It also introduces an offline reference at the feature level, which the authors associate with retaining the quality of sequential KL divergence. The approach brings together sparse feature usage and reference-based constraints, with the goal of simplifying alignment while keeping training stable and model changes controllable.

On benchmark datasets, the authors report an absolute win-rate improvement of more than five percentage points over state-of-the-art baselines, alongside substantially lower computational cost. These are empirical results for the evaluated comparisons. The contribution is evidence that constraints built around a well-trained sparse autoencoder can make preference alignment both more effective and less computationally demanding.
icml-2025-constrain-alignment-with-spars.tldr: FPO uses pretrained sparse-autoencoder features to constrain preference optimization, reporting better alignment win rates at substantially lower computational cost.

paragraphs: Masked image generation and masked diffusion begin from different motivations, but this paper shows that they can be studied within a common framework. The authors use that connection to examine training and sampling choices together. Their resulting model, eMIGM, incorporates improvements identified through this exploration of the shared design space.

The experiments evaluate image generation on ImageNet using Fréchet Inception Distance, or FID. At a resolution of 256 by 256 pixels, eMIGM outperforms VAR when model sizes and numbers of function evaluations are similar. Function evaluations count model calls during generation, so this comparison considers both model capacity and the amount of sampling work.

When capacity and sampling computation increase, eMIGM reaches performance comparable to REPA while using fewer than 45% as many function evaluations. At 512 by 512 pixels, it also outperforms EDM2. Together, these results show that the unified framework yields competitive measured image quality across the reported settings, with a particularly favorable model-call comparison against REPA.
icml-2025-effective-and-efficient-masked.tldr: eMIGM unifies masked generation and masked diffusion design, achieving strong ImageNet results with favorable sampling efficiency.

paragraphs: Click-through rate prediction estimates whether a user will click an item. Many models do this by learning interactions between embeddings of raw identifiers. The paper argues that heavy dependence on these interactions contributes to embedding collapse, where representations lose useful dimensional variety, and redundancy, where features carry overlapping information.

Supervised Feature Generation, or SFG, changes how those representations are learned. An encoder builds hidden embeddings for individual features, and a decoder uses the hidden representations to regenerate embeddings for all features. The training objective incorporates whether a click occurred, making the generation process directly responsive to the prediction task rather than relying only on a self-supervised reconstruction objective.

SFG is designed to integrate with most existing click-through rate models, allowing established architectures to adopt this generative approach. Across the evaluated datasets and base models, the authors report reduced embedding collapse and information redundancy alongside substantial predictive improvements. The findings support supervising feature generation as a way to improve both representation quality and the final click prediction.
icml-2025-from-feature-interaction-to-fe.tldr: SFG improves click prediction by training models to generate feature embeddings using click supervision, reducing reported representation collapse and redundancy.

paragraphs: Multi-view clustering combines several descriptions of the same samples. Many approaches use anchors to build relationships with samples, but overlook relationships among the anchors themselves. Another difficulty is that cluster ordering can differ across views, creating anchor misalignment that disrupts the graph representation and can destabilize later clustering.

DTP-SF-BVF learns geometric relationships among anchors through self-expression and incorporates them into the anchor-to-sample graph through topology learning. It also assigns each view a permutation mechanism that jointly rearranges anchors according to that view's characteristics. This alignment process does not require choosing one view as the baseline, and it operates together with anchor learning.

The method constructs cluster labels directly through binary assignments from the original samples, bypassing the spectral-embedding-and-partitioning stage discussed in the abstract. This design aims to preserve data diversity while avoiding variability introduced by that stage. Experiments on multiple public datasets support the method's effectiveness, combining richer graph relationships, coordinated anchor alignment, and direct cluster assignment in one framework.
icml-2025-from-spectrum-free-towards-bas.tldr: DTP-SF-BVF improves multi-view clustering by learning anchor relationships, aligning views without a baseline view, and assigning clusters directly.

paragraphs: Predicting counts requires representing uncertainty as well as estimating a numerical outcome. For continuous outcomes, Gaussian neural networks can let uncertainty vary flexibly with the input. This paper develops an analogous approach for discrete counts, where the desired uncertainty representation must remain compatible with count-valued predictions.

The Deep Double Poisson Network, or DDPN, predicts parameters of a Double Poisson distribution. This lets it represent very high or very low aleatoric uncertainty: variability inherent in the outcome for a given input. Combining multiple DDPNs into an ensemble also improves the estimation of epistemic uncertainty, which concerns uncertainty in the learned model.

The authors prove that DDPN has robust regression properties through learnable loss attenuation, a mechanism that adjusts how strongly prediction errors affect training, and introduce a loss modification to control it. Experiments on diverse datasets report improvements over existing baselines in prediction accuracy, uncertainty calibration, and detection of out-of-distribution inputs. These results connect flexible count uncertainty to benefits in both prediction and reliability assessment.
icml-2025-fully-heteroscedastic-count-re.tldr: DDPN gives count-prediction networks flexible input-dependent uncertainty, improving reported accuracy, calibration, and out-of-distribution detection.

paragraphs: Compositional generation asks a model to satisfy several conditions together. A generated sample may match parts of a request while missing the complete combination. This paper introduces a resampling criterion based on lift scores, using separate checks of the individual conditions to assess whether their composition has been satisfied.

The key practical insight is that these scores can be approximated efficiently using the original diffusion model itself. The approach does not require another training stage or an external module to assess condition alignment. The authors also develop an optimized version that reduces inference overhead relative to their approach while maintaining its effectiveness.

Experiments cover two-dimensional synthetic data, CLEVR position tasks, and text-to-image synthesis. Across these settings, the authors report significant improvements in how well generated samples align with composed conditions. The contribution is a way to guide resampling using the model's own information about individual requirements, with an optimized variant that makes the added inference work less costly.
icml-2025-improving-compositional-genera.tldr: Lift-score resampling improves diffusion models' adherence to combined conditions using the original model without additional training or external modules.

paragraphs: A language model asked to repeat one word many times can unexpectedly switch to unrelated text. This paper investigates the mechanism behind that failure, treating it as a way that users can push a model away from its intended behavior. The explanation centers on attention sinks, where the initial token attracts an unusually large share of attention.

The authors identify a neural circuit responsible for this attention pattern and show that long repetitions disrupt it. They also find nonrepeating sequences that produce similar disruptions. That extension matters because it connects the observed failure to a particular internal mechanism, rather than identifying repetition alone as the relevant surface feature.

Using this diagnosis, the authors propose a targeted patch and report that it resolves the issue without harming overall model performance. The study links an observable behavioral problem, a disrupted internal circuit, and a focused intervention. It demonstrates how mechanistic interpretability can contribute to repairing a specific reliability vulnerability in language models.
icml-2025-interpreting-the-repeated-toke.tldr: The paper traces repetition-induced language-model failures to disrupted attention-sink circuitry and reports a targeted patch that resolves the issue.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how to encourage a reinforcement learning agent to behave simply across an entire episode. Existing approaches can favor simpler policies, simpler representations of observations, or simpler objectives. The authors explore a complementary target: the structure of the sequence of states and actions produced as the agent performs its task.

Their approach modifies the learning problem to also maximize total correlation within these trajectories. Total correlation measures statistical dependence among variables; here, it provides a way to encourage structure across a trajectory. The motivation is that simplicity in an agent’s overall behavior could help it focus on patterns that remain useful when conditions change.

To make this objective practical, the authors propose an algorithm based on a lower-bound approximation. It optimizes the policy and the state representation along with the other models. This connects how the agent represents its situation and chooses its actions to the structure of the resulting behavior.

In simulated robot environments, the method produces periodic trajectories with patterns that repeat, as well as trajectories that are compressible. The resulting policies show greater robustness to noise and changes in dynamics than the baseline methods, while also improving performance on the original tasks. These findings support trajectory structure as a useful additional target for learning in the environments studied.
icml-2025-maximum-total-correlation-rein.tldr: Encouraging statistical dependence within an agent’s trajectories produces periodic, compressible behavior and improves task performance and robustness in simulated robot environments.

paragraphs: Diffusion models can generate plans, but standard diffusion planners have limited ways to turn additional inference computation into better solutions. Monte Carlo Tree Diffusion, or MCTD, addresses this by combining diffusion generation with Monte Carlo Tree Search. The aim is to make planning more deliberative as additional computation becomes available.

MCTD treats denoising as a branching search process. Partially denoised plans can be evaluated, pruned, and refined, allowing the search to allocate more effort to promising trajectories. It can also revisit and improve less successful branches. This gives the planner a way to balance exploring alternatives against developing candidates that already look useful.

On challenging long-horizon tasks, the authors report that MCTD outperforms diffusion baselines and produces better solutions as inference-time computation increases. The results support the value of organizing generation as adaptive search. Additional computation can then be directed toward evaluating and refining alternative plans within the diffusion process, rather than leaving the planner with only limited scaling options.
icml-2025-monte-carlo-tree-diffusion-for.tldr: MCTD turns diffusion denoising into adaptive tree search, improving long-horizon plans as inference computation increases in experiments.

paragraphs: Fast adversarial training aims to improve resistance to adversarial attacks while reducing training time. Its speed can come with weaker robustness because the training process does not sufficiently explore the adversarial space. This paper addresses that problem by changing the loss used during training, providing a modification that can accompany existing fast methods.

The authors derive a quadratic upper bound on the adversarial training loss. An upper bound provides a quantity that bounds the original objective from above; here, the proposed bound becomes a training loss used with fast adversarial training procedures. The contribution therefore focuses on the optimization objective within those procedures.

Experiments show significant robustness improvements when the quadratic upper-bound loss is applied to existing methods. The authors also examine several metrics and find evidence suggesting that a smoother loss landscape likely explains the gains. This proposed explanation remains qualified: the results support smoothing as a likely mechanism, alongside the directly reported empirical improvement in adversarial robustness.
icml-2025-quadratic-upper-bound-for-boos.tldr: A quadratic upper-bound loss improves existing fast adversarial training methods, with evidence suggesting smoother loss landscapes help explain the gains.

paragraphs: Compressing a large language model can make deployment on resource-limited devices more practical and help reduce computational demands. Radio approaches compression through quantization, which represents model weights more compactly. The paper develops a rate–distortion perspective for this problem, connecting the amount of information retained with the degradation introduced by compression.

The proposed method uses a simple rate–distortion optimization procedure. Its central purpose is to make the compression tradeoff controllable: a user can specify a desired model size or a desired accuracy. Those two options express different priorities, depending on whether the binding requirement is a storage budget or preservation of predictive quality.

The technique operates after training and scales to models with hundreds of billions of weight parameters. These stated capabilities make the contribution relevant to compressing already-trained models at substantial scale. The paper's main result is a theoretical foundation paired with a practical optimization approach for choosing a compression level according to a user-specified size or accuracy target.
icml-2025-radio-ratedistortion-optimizat.tldr: Radio uses rate–distortion optimization to compress pretrained language models toward user-specified size or accuracy targets.

paragraphs: Self-attributing neural networks incorporate explanations into their own predictions, but doing so can come at a performance cost in high-dimensional problems. This paper investigates whether explaining predictions through individual features creates constraints that grouping features can overcome. Its theoretical analysis establishes an error lower bound for per-feature models and shows that group-based models can achieve zero error.

Motivated by that distinction, Sum-of-Parts, or SOP, turns any differentiable model into a group-based self-attributing network. The feature groups are learned jointly with the model rather than supplied through group annotations. This allows the explanatory units to emerge during training, making learned combinations of features central to the model's attribution structure.

The authors report state-of-the-art performance among self-attributing networks on vision and language tasks. Quantitative and semantic evaluations support the interpretability of the learned groups, and additional applications demonstrate their usefulness for debugging models and cosmological scientific discovery. Together, these results support feature grouping as a way to improve the balance between predictive performance and built-in explanations.
icml-2025-sum-of-parts-self-attributing-.tldr: SOP learns feature groups end to end to give differentiable models built-in explanations with strong reported predictive performance.

paragraphs: Test-time adaptation adjusts predictions using unlabeled test data when the deployment distribution differs from training. Access to source data may be restricted, making source correlations unavailable. This paper investigates whether correlations among high-certainty test instances can instead provide a useful alignment reference for the broader test population.

The authors give a theoretical analysis supporting performance improvement through this form of correlation alignment. LinearTCA implements the idea with a linear transformation that aligns both instances and correlations without further model updates. LinearTCA+ provides a plug-in version for existing adaptation methods, allowing the same principle to supplement their adaptation procedures.

Across evaluated tasks, benchmarks, and backbones, the methods outperform the compared baselines. LinearTCA achieves higher accuracy while using 4% of the GPU memory and 0.6% of the computation time of the best TTA baseline in the reported comparison. The authors also report an improvement exceeding 1.86% over existing methods on CLIP. These findings combine predictive gains with a particularly low computational burden for the update-free variant.
icml-2025-test-time-correlation-alignmen.tldr: Test-time correlation alignment uses high-certainty instances as a reference, improving reported adaptation accuracy with very low computational cost.

paragraphs: Automated computational phenotypes can be obtained much faster than manually extracted gold-standard phenotype labels. However, substituting automated outputs directly for those labels can bias downstream analyses. This paper studies how to use the automated information while preserving valid statistical inference when gold-standard labels are available for only part of the data.

The setting is semi-supervised and allows covariate shift between populations. The authors develop doubly robust, semiparametrically efficient estimators for general target parameters in the unlabeled population and in the combined population. These properties concern robustness and statistical efficiency within the stated framework, making the automated phenotypes inputs to a principled estimation procedure rather than unquestioned replacement labels.

The analysis compares estimation efficiency with and without automated phenotypes and identifies a specific source of benefit: automated phenotypes for the unlabeled data drive the additional efficiency gains. Synthetic experiments and applications to several real-world datasets support the theoretical findings. The result clarifies both how to incorporate automated phenotypes and which part of the data supplies their statistical value.
icml-2025-towards-the-efficient-inferenc.tldr: The paper develops efficient estimators under covariate shift and identifies automated phenotypes on unlabeled data as the source of added efficiency.

paragraphs: Predicting an electronic-structure Hamiltonian requires respecting how physical quantities change when a system rotates. TraceGrad aims to combine strict three-dimensional rotation equivariance with expressive nonlinear learning. Equivariance means that rotating the input produces the corresponding transformation in the output, preserving the relationship required by the physical prediction task.

The framework first derives rotation-invariant trace quantities from the target Hamiltonians and uses them as supervision. These quantities remain unchanged under rotation. Because nonlinear operations preserve invariance, the model can use rich nonlinear mappings while learning invariant features, capturing complex patterns without breaking that symmetry property.

A gradient-based mechanism then converts the learned invariant features into equivariant encodings of different degrees. The construction theoretically preserves equivariance while connecting the expressive learned features to representations appropriate for the regression targets. Experiments on eight benchmark databases report state-of-the-art Hamiltonian prediction performance. The contribution is a route from nonlinear invariant learning to symmetry-respecting outputs, supported by both the construction's theoretical properties and the reported prediction results.
icml-2025-tracegrad-a-framework-learning.tldr: TraceGrad learns nonlinear rotation-invariant features and converts them through gradients into equivariant representations for accurate Hamiltonian prediction.

paragraphs: A world model predicts how an environment changes, but sharing one across environments becomes difficult when their sensors and actuators differ. This paper addresses that problem for low-dimensional sensor information. It tackles both the diversity of pretraining data and the architectural flexibility needed to use data from heterogeneous control environments.

The authors introduce UniTraj, a dataset containing more than one million trajectories from 80 environments. They pair it with TrajWorld, an architecture that accommodates varying sensor and actuator information and learns environment dynamics from context. The dataset supplies diverse experience, while the model is designed to handle differences in how environments are observed and controlled.

Pretraining TrajWorld on UniTraj improves transition prediction, establishes a reported state of the art for off-policy evaluation, and improves online model predictive control performance. These results connect predictive transfer with downstream evaluation and control benefits. The authors describe the work, to their knowledge, as the first demonstration of such transfer benefits across heterogeneous, complex control environments.
icml-2025-trajectory-world-models-for-he.tldr: UniTraj and TrajWorld enable world-model pretraining across differing sensors and actuators, improving reported prediction, policy evaluation, and control.

paragraphs: Wasserstein distance compares distributions, but its computational cost can make repeated comparisons burdensome. Tree-Wasserstein distance offers a linear-time approximation using a tree representation. The quality of that approximation depends on the tree's structure and edge weights, which existing approaches can choose suboptimally.

UltraTWD learns both parts together through an unsupervised optimization framework. It constructs ultrametric trees that aim to represent the underlying cost matrix more faithfully. Its algorithms combine minimum spanning trees, iterative projection, and gradient descent to learn the structure and weights efficiently. This treats the tree as an object to optimize rather than simply a fixed approximation device.

Experiments involving document retrieval, ranking, and classification show improved approximation accuracy and competitive performance on the downstream tasks. These are related but distinct findings: a closer approximation to the distributional distance is useful, while practical task performance tests whether that representation serves an application. UltraTWD contributes a way to improve the learned approximation while retaining the appeal of tree-based distance computation.
icml-2025-ultratwd-optimizing-ultrametri.tldr: UltraTWD jointly optimizes tree structure and edge weights to improve tree-Wasserstein approximation accuracy.

paragraphs: During neural-network training, the loss landscape around the current parameters often becomes sharper before leveling off near the edge of stability. This progressive sharpening is widely observed, yet its mechanisms remain difficult to explain. The paper studies it using a deliberately minimal network with multiple linear layers and just one neuron in each layer.

Despite its simplicity, this model reproduces sharpness dynamics seen in recent empirical studies. That makes it a manageable setting for theoretical analysis. The authors examine how properties of the dataset, network depth, optimizer randomness, and step size influence the extent of progressive sharpening within this minimal model.

They then present empirical evidence that insights from the analysis extend to practical training scenarios. The theoretical results concern the simplified model, while the broader relevance is supported experimentally. The contribution is a tractable testbed for understanding how data, architecture, and optimization interact during training, helping explain a pattern that would otherwise be difficult to isolate in a full-scale neural network.
icml-2025-understanding-sharpness-dynami.tldr: A minimal deep linear network explains how data, depth, optimizer randomness, and step size shape progressive sharpening during training.

paragraphs: Large vision-language models understand images and text, but their general knowledge does not automatically align with the visual patterns needed for deepfake detection. This paper builds a framework that connects those capabilities to forgery evidence. It combines a specialized detector, a prompt-learning component, and a language model that produces textual detection responses.

The Knowledge-guided Forgery Detector compares image features with embeddings of descriptions of pristine and manipulated images. These correlations support both classification and localization of forgery evidence. A Forgery Prompt Learner then converts the detector's outputs into detailed prompt embeddings, which reach the language model together with visual information and the user's question.

Experiments across FF++, CDF2, DFD, DFDCP, DFDC, and DF40 report stronger generalization than state-of-the-art methods. The framework also supports multi-turn dialogue, allowing detection to be presented through an interactive language interface. Its contribution is a structured connection between visual forgery analysis and language generation, with reported benefits for generalization and the ability to communicate detection results.
icml-2025-unlocking-the-capabilities-of-.tldr: The framework connects localized forgery evidence to a vision-language model, improving reported deepfake generalization and supporting conversational detection responses.

paragraphs: In-context learning lets a language model infer a task from a few demonstrations in its prompt. Two proposed mechanisms explain this ability differently. Induction heads locate and copy relevant tokens, while function-vector heads represent the task through an internal encoding. This paper compares their roles across 12 language models.

Detailed ablation experiments indicate that function-vector heads are the primary drivers of few-shot in-context learning, particularly in larger models. Ablations test the contribution of model components by disrupting them and observing the behavioral effect. The findings therefore help distinguish components associated with in-context learning from those that contribute more strongly to its measured performance.

The authors also examine how these mechanisms develop during training. Many function-vector heads initially behave as induction heads before transitioning to the function-vector mechanism. Based on that connection, they speculate that induction helps the model learn the more complex mechanism. The developmental observation supports this possibility, while the proposed facilitating role remains an interpretation rather than an established causal conclusion.
icml-2025-which-attention-heads-matter-f.tldr: Ablations across 12 language models identify function-vector heads as the main drivers of few-shot in-context learning, especially in larger models.

paragraphs: Embodied agents must adapt when the environments they act in change, ideally without extensive new data collection or retraining. WorMI addresses this through test-time composition: it connects a language model's reasoning capabilities with independently learned world models that contain knowledge specific to different domains. Those world models can be inserted and removed as needed.

The framework retrieves relevant models by matching abstract trajectory representations against prototypes. It then uses a compound attention mechanism to combine information from the retrieved world models and align their intermediate representations with the reasoning model's representations. This alignment lets separately learned sources of environmental knowledge contribute within the agent's policy.

Evaluations on VirtualHome and ALFWorld show stronger zero-shot and few-shot performance than several language-model-based approaches across unseen domains. The results support retrieving and composing world models as a route to adaptation in those benchmarks. The authors present scalable real-world deployment as a potential application, building on the demonstrated ability to combine domain knowledge at test time.
icml-2025-world-model-implanting-for-tes.tldr: WorMI retrieves and integrates domain-specific world models at test time to improve embodied agents' adaptation to unseen environments.
